passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of caffeine on reaction time in a controlled laboratory setting. One hundred healthy adults were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a placebo (control) group, a low-dose caffeine group (50 mg), a medium-dose caffeine group (100 mg), and a high-dose caffeine group (200 mg). Each participant completed a computerized simple reaction time task 30 minutes after ingestion. The task required pressing a button as quickly as possible when a visual stimulus appeared on the screen. Mean reaction times (RT) and standard deviations (SD) were recorded for each group. The researchers hypothesized that moderate caffeine intake would improve reaction speed, whereas excessive intake might produce a plateau or even a decline due to overstimulation. The study also monitored heart rate and subjective alertness to assess potential side effects. Results indicated a dose-dependent improvement in RT up to 100 mg, after which the benefit plateaued. No significant differences were observed in heart rate or alertness scores between groups. These findings suggest that moderate caffeine consumption can enhance cognitive performance without adverse cardiovascular effects.
table_data:
Condition | Mean RT (ms) | SD
Control | 350 | 20
Low Dose | 330 | 18
Medium Dose | 310 | 15
High Dose | 310 | 17
stem: Based on the data presented, which statement best describes the relationship between caffeine dose and reaction time?

options.A: Reaction time improves linearly with increasing caffeine dose.
options.B: Reaction time improves up to 100 mg, then plateaus.
options.C: Reaction time worsens at the highest caffeine dose.
options.D: There is no significant difference in reaction time across doses.

explanation: The table shows mean RT decreasing from 350 ms (control) to 310 ms at both 100 mg and 200 mg, indicating improvement up to 100 mg and a plateau thereafter.
trap: Option A suggests a continuous linear improvement, which is contradicted by the plateau at 200 mg.

stem: If the researchers wanted to determine whether caffeine’s effect on reaction time is dose-dependent, which experimental design modification would be most appropriate?

options.A: Add a group receiving 150 mg of caffeine to create a finer dose gradient.
options.B: Replace the reaction time task with a memory recall task.
options.C: Increase the sample size to 200 participants per group.
options.D: Administer caffeine orally instead of intravenously.

explanation: Adding a 150 mg group provides an intermediate dose, allowing the researchers to better characterize the dose-response curve and confirm the plateau hypothesis.
trap: Option C focuses on sample size but does not address dose-dependency directly.

stem: What is the percent reduction in mean reaction time when comparing the control group to the medium-dose caffeine group?
trap: Option C (10.3%) appears close but is not the exact percent reduction.

stem: Which of the following is a potential confounding variable that could bias the study’s findings?

options.A: Time of day when the test was administered.
options.B: The color of the laboratory walls.
options.C: The brand of the computer used for the task.

explanation: Circadian rhythms influence alertness and reaction time; if not controlled, time of day could confound caffeine effects.
trap: Option B is irrelevant and distracts from the actual confounder.

stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the table?

options.A: Increasing the dose from 100 mg to 200 mg gave no further reduction in mean reaction time.
options.B: The 200 mg dose slowed reaction time relative to 100 mg.
options.C: Caffeine reduced heart rate compared with placebo.

explanation: Correct: Mean RT was 310 ms at both 100 mg and 200 mg, so the higher dose added no further speed benefit. Why the others are wrong: B) Both doses had the same mean RT. C) The passage says heart rate did not differ between groups. D) Memory was not measured.
trap: Assuming a higher dose must give a bigger effect, or generalizing a simple reaction-time result to memory, which was not measured.
